subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Which factor increases the thinking distance?
questions.explain: Thinking distance depends on reaction time, increased by tiredness, alcohol or distractions. Worn brakes, ice and bald tyres increase the braking distance instead.

questions.q: Which statement about permanent and induced magnets is correct?
options: Induced magnetism produces a force of repulsion
A permanent magnet loses its magnetism as soon as it is moved away from iron
An induced magnet only becomes magnetic in a magnetic field and quickly loses it when removed
An induced magnet always repels a permanent magnet
questions.explain: Induced magnetism appears only while a material is in a magnetic field and is lost (or much reduced) when removed. Induced magnets always cause attraction, never repulsion.

questions.q: Hooke's law states that, up to the limit of proportionality, the extension of a spring is:
options: Directly proportional to the force applied
questions.explain: Hooke's law: extension is directly proportional to the force, so F = ke. This holds only up to the limit of proportionality, beyond which the relationship is no longer linear.

questions.q: An object has a resultant force of zero acting on it. What can you conclude?
options: It is either stationary or moving at constant velocity
questions.explain: Zero resultant force means no acceleration, so the object stays still or keeps moving at constant velocity (Newton's first law).

questions.q: What is the cause of the upthrust that a fluid exerts on a submerged object?
options: The object's weight pushes the fluid up
Pressure is greater on the bottom of the object than on the top
Pressure is the same everywhere on the object
questions.explain: Pressure in a fluid increases with depth, so the upward pressure on the bottom of the object is greater than the downward pressure on the top. This pressure difference gives a net upward force called upthrust.

questions.q: For an object in a circular orbit, in which direction does the gravitational force act?
options: There is no force on an orbiting object
Towards the centre of the orbit, acting as the centripetal force
Away from the centre of the orbit
questions.explain: Gravity acts towards the centre of the orbit, providing the centripetal force that keeps the object moving in a circle and constantly changing direction.

questions.q: A runner completes one full lap of a 400 m circular track, finishing where they started. What is their displacement?
questions.explain: Displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish (a vector). Finishing at the start gives 0 m displacement, even though the distance travelled is 400 m.

questions.q: A see-saw is balanced. A child of weight 300 N sits 1.0 m from the pivot. Where must a 150 N child sit on the other side to balance it?
questions.explain: For balance, the moments are equal: 300 × 1.0 = 150 × d, so d = 300/150 = 2.0 m. The lighter child must sit further from the pivot.

questions.q: For a stable orbit, if a satellite moves to a larger orbital radius, what must happen to its speed?
options: It cannot stay in orbit at a larger radius
Its speed stays exactly the same
questions.explain: For a stable orbit at a given radius there is only one possible speed. A larger orbital radius requires a slower orbital speed; a smaller radius requires a faster speed.

questions.q: Which statement about force is correct?
options: Force is a vector with both magnitude and direction
Force is a scalar with magnitude only
Force has direction but no size
questions.explain: Force is a vector quantity: it has both a magnitude and a direction, and is measured in newtons (N). This is why forces are drawn as arrows.

questions.q: An object moves at a steady speed in a circular orbit. Why is it still accelerating?
options: Its direction (and therefore velocity) is constantly changing
It is moving in a straight line
questions.explain: Velocity is a vector. Even at constant speed, the direction is continuously changing in a circular orbit, so the velocity changes — this change in velocity is the (centripetal) acceleration.

questions.q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explain: A vector has both magnitude and direction. Velocity has direction, so it is a vector; mass, temperature and speed are scalars (magnitude only).

questions.q: As you go deeper into a liquid, what happens to the pressure?
questions.explain: Pressure in a fluid increases with depth because there is a greater weight of fluid above pushing down (p = hρg).

questions.q: What does it mean if a spring is stretched beyond its limit of proportionality?
options: The extension is no longer directly proportional to the force
No more force is needed to stretch it
questions.explain: Beyond the limit of proportionality the force–extension graph is no longer a straight line, so extension is no longer directly proportional to force (and deformation may become inelastic).

questions.q: Which of these is the correct SI base unit of mass?
questions.explain: The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram (kg). The gram is a smaller unit, the newton is the unit of force, and the pound is not an SI unit.

questions.q: What happens to atmospheric pressure as you climb to a higher altitude?
questions.explain: As altitude increases there is less air above you, so the weight pressing down is smaller and atmospheric pressure decreases.

questions.q: An object floats when the upthrust acting on it is:
questions.explain: When floating, the upthrust (upward force from the fluid) balances the object's weight, so the resultant force is zero. If weight exceeds the maximum upthrust, the object sinks.

questions.q: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the volume is halved. According to pV = constant, the new pressure is...
questions.explain: At constant temperature pV is constant, so if V is halved, p must double to keep the product the same (Boyle's law).

questions.q: A book rests on a table. The table pushes up on the book. Which is the Newton's third law pair to this force?
options: The weight of the book pulling down
The air pressure on the book
The book pushing down on the table
questions.explain: Newton's third law pairs are equal, opposite, act on different objects and are the same type of force (contact). The table pushing up on the book pairs with the book pushing down on the table.

questions.q: What keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
options: The gravitational force of attraction from the Sun
questions.explain: Gravity provides the force that keeps planets in orbit. The Sun's large mass produces a gravitational attraction acting on each planet.

questions.q: An object is partly submerged in water. What causes the upthrust on it?
options: The water pressure is greater on the bottom than on the top of the object
The object is lighter than air
questions.explain: Pressure in a fluid increases with depth, so the upward pressure on the bottom of the object is greater than the downward pressure on its top. This difference produces a net upward force called upthrust.

questions.q: A spring returns exactly to its original length after a stretching force is removed. This deformation is described as:
questions.explain: Elastic deformation means the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed. If it stays deformed, the deformation is inelastic (plastic).
